whyThisMatters: Most security myths survive because they are half true. They sound sensible to smart people, which is exactly why they are dangerous. Spotting where each one breaks down is what separates a habit from a guess.
rememberThis: A control that works in one situation is not a guarantee in all of them. The padlock, MFA, a VPN and a strong password each solve one specific problem. Ask what exactly it protects, and what it leaves open.

discussionPrompts: Ask who would have said TRUE to the padlock or MFA myths before today. What did the padlock or the phone prompt actually prove, and what did it leave open?
Ask: if an attacker had your email password right now, what is the first thing they could do without ever touching your laptop?
For the password manager myth, ask the group to compare the two failure modes: one strong vault with MFA versus the same password reused on twenty sites. Which is easier for an attacker to exploit?
Ask whether anyone has ever 'deleted' a file and later found it in a recycle bin, backup or sync folder. What does that say about where the data really lives?
Ask how you would know if your account had been quietly accessed for a week. What signals would you actually see?
facilitatorNotes.commonWrongAnswer: People most often get mf-02 wrong. MFA is such a strong control that 'MFA means safe' feels almost true, and it is the closest myth to reality. The correction is that MFA defeats password theft but not approval fatigue, adversary-in-the-middle phishing or stolen session tokens. People also commonly accept mf-01 because the padlock is taught as a safety signal.

items.myth: If a website shows the padlock and starts with HTTPS, it is a trustworthy site.
items.fact: HTTPS only proves that your connection to that domain is encrypted and that the domain holds a certificate. It says nothing about who owns the domain or whether they are honest. Free certificates are available to anyone, including phishing sites.
items.detail: Why: encryption protects the road, not the destination. A lookalike domain such as acme-payroll-login.com can have a perfectly valid certificate. Check the domain name itself, and go to sensitive sites from a bookmark or typed address rather than a link.

items.myth: With multi-factor authentication switched on, my account cannot be taken over.
items.fact: MFA blocks the common case of a stolen password being used alone, but determined attackers work around it. They flood you with prompts until you approve one, or they relay your login through a fake page and steal the session afterwards.
items.detail: Why: MFA fatigue relies on a tired person tapping Approve. Adversary-in-the-middle (AiTM) phishing proxies the real login page and captures your session token, which is already past the MFA step. Deny prompts you did not start, report them, and prefer phishing-resistant methods such as passkeys or security keys.

items.myth: A password manager puts all my passwords in one place, so it is a single point of failure and riskier than remembering them myself.
items.fact: The real comparison is not one vault versus perfect memory. It is one well-protected vault versus the passwords people reuse and weaken when they have to remember them. For most people the vault is far safer.
items.detail: Why: reused passwords fall to credential stuffing, where a leak on one site is tried automatically on others. A vault is encrypted with a key derived from your master password, and sites should only store a salted hash of what you give them. Protect the vault with a long master passphrase and MFA.

items.myth: Once I delete a file and empty the recycle bin, the data is gone.
items.fact: Deleting usually removes the pointer to the file, not the content itself. Copies often remain in backups, cloud sync, email attachments and on the disk until it is overwritten.
items.detail: Why: file systems mark space as free rather than erasing it, and sync and backup tools deliberately keep versions. For sensitive data, use the approved secure-disposal or wipe process, and remember that a file you emailed or shared is not under your control any more.

items.myth: Private or incognito browsing hides what I do from my employer.
items.fact: Incognito only stops your own browser saving history and cookies on that device. Your employer's network, proxy and monitoring tools, the websites you visit and your internet provider can all still see the traffic.
items.detail: Why: privacy mode is about local storage, not network visibility. Traffic on a work network or device passes through systems the company controls. Assume work devices and connections are monitored within policy, and keep personal activity off them.

items.myth: If my account or laptop were hacked, I would notice.
items.fact: Attackers are usually quiet. Many compromises go unnoticed for weeks because the goal is access, not disruption, and nothing visibly breaks.
items.detail: Why: a mailbox rule that silently forwards copies of your email, or a stolen session token, produces no warning on your screen. Look at the signals you can see, such as unexpected sign-in alerts, unfamiliar devices in your account, or colleagues replying to emails you never sent, and report them.

items.myth: Phishing emails are easy to spot because they are full of spelling mistakes and awkward grammar.
items.fact: Modern phishing is often flawless, written with AI tools, and tailored to your role. Targeted messages quote real projects and use a real colleague's writing style.
items.detail: Why: attackers copy genuine messages and research targets, a technique called spear phishing. Judge the request, not the prose. Is it unexpected, urgent, asking for credentials, money or a change to normal process? Verify through a separate channel.

items.myth: Only large, famous companies get attacked. A mid-sized business like ours is too small to be worth it.
items.fact: Most attacks are automated and indiscriminate. Smaller organisations are often chosen because they have fewer defences, and they can also be a route to bigger partners.
items.detail: Why: scanners probe the whole internet for unpatched systems, and exploits are often used within days of a fix being published. That gap is the patching window. Attackers also run stolen passwords against every company in credential-stuffing waves. Size is not what they select on; weakness is.

items.myth: A VPN makes me anonymous and safe on any website.
items.fact: A VPN encrypts traffic between your device and the VPN server and hides your location from the local network. It does not stop phishing, malware or the sites you log in to from knowing who you are.
items.detail: Why: the VPN provider can see your traffic instead of the cafe, and once you sign in to an account you are identified anyway. A malicious download or fake login page works just as well through a tunnel. A VPN fixes one risk, untrusted networks, and nothing else.

items.myth: If a caller knows my name, my manager and what project I am on, they must be genuine.
items.fact: Knowing those details proves only that the caller did some research. Public profiles, old emails and leaked data make that information easy to collect.
items.detail: Why: this is pretexting, building a believable story from real facts to earn trust. The defence is process, not instinct. Hang up and call back on a number you already hold, and never read out codes or passwords because someone sounds informed.
